html:
A cookbook compiled in Baghdad in the 10th century by Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq. Its title means "The Book of Dishes", and it is the oldest Arabic cookbook that survives.

It gathers over 600 recipes, many taken from the kitchens of the Abbasid caliphs and their courtiers. Some are credited to the prince Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi, a famous gourmet and half brother of Harun al-Rashid. There are stews, roasts, breads, pickles, sweets and drinks, with spices, sugar, rose water and nuts.

The book also gives advice on health, following the Greek theory of the four humours, on table manners and on kitchen tools. It shows the mix of Persian, Arab and Greek traditions at the Abbasid court at its height. Few manuscripts survive, and an English translation appeared only in 2007. Compare the Roman Apicius collection, several centuries older.
